world's structure by the sheet's own price record — the face looked up by
claim, the cost `face * price_bp // 10000`, the discount `10000 - price_bp`.

    The entry is refused by name when the quote record carries no `claim`,
    `dated` or `price_bp`, when the claim is not on the capital structure,
    when the price is negative or at or above par, and when the dated is not
    one of the two dates the sheet prints.
"""

import claims

PAR_BP = 10000

ENTRY_KEYS = ("claim", "dated", "price_bp", "face_cents", "cost_cents",
              "discount_bp")


class EntryError(ValueError):
    """The refusal this stage raises: something that cannot be a trade.

    It names the offender — the quote record that carried no price, the claim
    the structure does not hold, the price at or above par, the date the sheet
    never printed — because a trade the market cannot have made must say what
    it was asked for rather than answer a position nobody underwrote.
    """


def entry(claims, quote):
    """The trade the sheet priced: face, print, cost in cents, discount in bp.

    `quote` is a `QUOTE_KEYS` record off the world's sheet — one claim, one of
    the two printed dates, one price in basis points of par. The stage looks
    the claim's face up on the capital structure and answers the record: the
    print echoed, the cost truncated from `face * price_bp // 10000`, the
    discount the price leaves against par.

    A print at or above par is refused by name: that trade is the waterfall's
    to pay, not the entry's to price. A claim off the structure, a price off
    the sheet or a date off the sheet is refused by name too.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement entry()")
files.stage_03.py:
"""Distressed Debt Investing From Scratch — stage 3: Expected recovery from what actually happened.

The buy side of this course cannot read the world's answer key — the outcome
the close recorded is the thing the grades in stage 10 are marked against — so
it needs a recovery estimate it can defend without it. This stage builds one
out of the only facts a fund may use: what the bank's own lending on the same
segment ACTUALLY collected when it defaulted.

The book (`book.py`, the bank's own world) holds the defaulted loans, their
principal and their recovery cash flows. The stage filters that book down to
the loans that defaulted on the segment the claim rides — `loan["segment"] ==
claim["segment"]` — and only the ones with recoveries to read: a defaulted
loan that collected nothing still contributes its par, but a segment where
nothing has yet defaulted cannot answer a rate at all, and is refused by name.

Every recovery row feeds the walk. A row the book marked `collateral` rides
its loan's collateral haircut (`rules.COLLATERAL_HAIRCUT_BP`, keyed by the
loan's own collateral kind) — the recovery is on the asset, less the haircut
the policy books on it. Every row is then discounted to `at` the distance of
`months_between(at, row_date)` months, one factor step at a time the way M1's
own world discounts — `factor = factor * 10000 // (10000 + period_rate)` —
with the rate each loan was written at. A recovery collected before `at` rides
undiscounted (zero months); one collected after `at` is discounted forward,
the distance of the months between them. The answer is `discounted_cents`
over the segment's defaulted par: a rate in basis points of par, and the
cents that rate gives the claim's own face.

    FORECAST_KEYS                 the nine fields of an expected recovery, in order
    ForecastError                 the refusal this stage raises
    expected_recovery(book, claim, at)
                                  -> FORECAST_KEYS, off the bank's actuals only

DESIGN DECISION — why is the walk matched on the segment, not on the collateral?
Because the claim rides a book segment — Berthline's distressed paper is
corporate lending — and the bank's defaulted corporate loans are the actuals
any corporate claim of that borrower could cite. Matching on the collateral
kind as well would leave the unsecured and the subordinated bonds unable to
cite anything (the bank's secured corporate loan is the only defaulted one of
them), and a forecast that refuses to answer for three of the four claims
informs nobody. The haircut stays collateral-by-collateral: each recovery row
is cut by its OWN loan's collateral kind, since the haircut is a policy on the
asset backing that loan, not on the claim reading the segment.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a recovery after `at` discount, and one before ride
flat?
Because the walk discounts a recovery the distance of months it sits from the
day the forecast is made, in whichever direction: a recovery the fund expects
in five months is worth the stepped factor, and one the bank already banked is
worth its amount — it arrived. The world's actuals were collected before the
fund's entry date, so they ride undiscounted there, and a check pins the
forward direction from an earlier `at`: the same walk evaluated before the
recoveries happened must discount them, one factor step per month, and answer
the lower rate.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the factor stepped one recovery at a time and never
powered?
Because the factor is a truncated integer in ten-thousandths —
`factor = factor * 10000 // (10000 + period_rate)` — and a power would either
float it or explode it. Stepping keeps every integer inside the scale of the
recovery it is applied to, keeps the arithmetic reproducible by hand, and
lands the discount discontinuously at exactly the months the calendar says.
It is the same shape the bank's own present values took, and this course
refuses to invent a second one.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the answer both a rate and the cents the claim would
recover?
Because the record serves two callers: the stages that reason about the
segment (the three-reading stage needs the rate to lay beside the Merton and
comparables views) and the stages that reason about the claim (the thesis
needs the cents the fund's face would recover on this view). The rate is
`discounted * 10000 // par` of the segment's defaulted book — the reading that
reproduces by hand; the cents apply that rate, truncated, to the claim's own
face. Both answer to the cent, and neither is rounded a second time.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the equity refused outright?
Because an equity claim rides no par: there is no face for a recovery rate to
apply to, and the book's lending never sold claims against the sponsor's
upside. A fund that "forecast a recovery" on its equity would be pricing the
going concern, which is the valuation machinery of another world. The refusal
names the claim, so the mistake is visible at the call rather than buried in a
rate applied to zero.

TODO: implement `ForecastError` and `expected_recovery` in this file: the
segment's own defaulted book, haircutted and discounted to `at`, answering a
rate in basis points of par and the cents that rate gives the claim's face.

    The request is refused by name when the claim record carries no `kind`,
    `segment` or `face_cents`, when the kind is `equity`, when the book's
    segment has no defaulted loan with recoveries to read, and when `at` is
    not a date the calendar accepts.
"""

import os
import sys

_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
_PATH = os.path.dirname(_DIR) if os.path.basename(_DIR) == "solutions" else _DIR
if _PATH not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, _PATH)

import dates
import rules
import claims as market

PAR_BP = 10000

FORECAST_KEYS = ("claim", "at", "segment", "collateral_kind", "loans",
                 "par_cents", "discounted_cents", "expected_cents", "expected_bp")


class ForecastError(ValueError):
    """The refusal this stage raises: something that cannot be a forecast.

    It names the offender — the claim the book cannot read, the segment with
    no defaulted loan behind it, the date the calendar does not accept —
    because a recovery estimate nobody can trace to actuals must say what it
    was asked for rather than answer a number nobody can underwrite on.
    """


def _months_between(start, end):
    """The whole months from `start` to `end`, the calendar's clamping honoured.

    A flow landing on the day itself is zero months away, and a start on a
    day the target month does not have still answers the floor the calendar's
    own `add_months` puts under it.
    """
    year, month, _day = dates.parse(start)
    other_year, other_month, _other_day = dates.parse(end)
    months = (other_year - year) * rules.PERIODS_PER_YEAR + (other_month - month)
    if months > 0 and dates.add_months(start, months) > end:
        months = months - 1
    if months < 0 and dates.add_months(start, months) < end:
        months = months + 1
    return months


def expected_recovery(book, claim, at):
    """The recovery rate the bank's own defaulted book gives the claim's segment.

    The walk reads every defaulted loan on `claim["segment"]` that collected
    anything: its principal counted into the segment's par, its recovery rows
    haircutted where they came from collateral and discounted to `at` at the
    loan's own rate, one truncating factor step per month of distance. The
    answer is the discounted cents over the par, in basis points of it, and
    those cents applied to the claim's own face.

    A claim of kind `equity`, a record the book cannot read, a segment with no
    defaulted loan to read and a date `at` the calendar refuses, is refused by
    name.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement expected_recovery()")
files.stage_04.py:
"""Distressed Debt Investing From Scratch — stage 4: Merton distance-to-default.

The recovery views so far all read the book. This stage reads the identity: is
the borrower actually going to be in the waterfall? The Merton machinery asks
it in one ratio — how far the borrower's assets stand above its debt, in units
of the volatility band the identity books it at — and this stage computes that
ratio in whole units, no floats, no standard deviations, no simulator.

The inputs are data: the asset value the borrower's path records, the debt the
identity's debt table books, and a volatility band in basis points that must be
one of the tabulated bands' own upper bounds — `calm` ends at fifteen hundred,
`normal` at thirty-two, `stressed` at fifty-four hundred, and a borrower is
booked at a band, not between two of them. The distance is

    dd_units = (asset - debt) * DD_SCALE * DD_SCALE // (asset * band_bp)

— the equity cushion over the par of the assets, measured in band units, at
the same fixed-point scale the bank's arithmetic already ran at. A borrower
whose debt stands at or above its assets answers a negative distance: the
waterfall is already deciding, and the distance says so honestly.

`to_pd(dd_units)` maps the distance to a cumulative probability of default,
and refuses to invent a row: the mapping is the `PD_LADDER` the world carries,
walked exactly like the bank's own migration buckets — the row whose
`from_dd` is the greatest lower bound of the distance answers — and a distance
below the ladder's first bound or above its last is refused by name. The
Merton view of recovery is then `10000 - pd_bp`, what the model expects the
par to be worth if it is not all wiped out.

    DD_SCALE                      the fixed-point scale the distance runs at
    MertonError                   the refusal this stage raises
    dd(asset_value, debt, band_bp)
                                  -> the distance in whole band units
    to_pd(dd_units)               -> the cumulative PD in basis points, off the
                                     world's own ladder

DESIGN DECISION — why must the band be a tabulated upper bound?
Because a band the identity books but the table does not hold is not a band —
it is a shrug. The bands table is the volatility the model knows how to mean:
three rows, three upper bounds, and a borrower's own bookings are exactly such
values. A distance computed at some in-between band (twenty-five, say) would
be an answer the ladder cannot grade and the check cannot recompute from the
world, so it is refused by name — the band the caller meant is in the
message, and the fix is to book the borrower properly.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the distance an integer fixed-point ratio instead of
a signed float with a normal distribution?
Because a float distance invites a float probability — a curve fitted to a
ladder — and this course's probabilities are tabulated, walked like the bank's
own buckets. The integer ratio keeps the monotone behaviour the identity
claims (more debt, or a wider band, pushes the distance down) with arithmetic
a reviewer reproduces, and it lands in the same units the PD ladder is walked
in. Where a real model would smooth the ends, the ladder refuses: the ends
are the world's, not this stage's.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the distance allow debt above assets instead of
refusing it?
Because negative distance is information, not a broken input: an asset value
the path recorded below the borrower's debt means the option is already
exercised and the waterfall is deciding, and `to_pd` will answer the ladder's
worst row for it (or refuse if the distance sinks past even that row). Only a
nonsense input — a non-positive asset, a non-positive debt — is refused at
`dd` itself, since a borrower with no assets or no debt is not a credit.

DESIGN DECISION — why is `to_pd` a separate walk rather than a column of `dd`?
Because the mapping from distance to probability is the world's data and not
this stage's arithmetic: the ladder arrives from the world, the greatest
lower-bound walk is the bank's own bucket semantics, and a check that wants to
prove the stage is honest walks the same ladder itself. Keeping the two
functions apart also lets the check pin the ladder's edges from both sides —
at each `from_dd` the row's own probability answers, one unit below the
previous row's does — which is exactly where a hand-rolled mapping would
drift off the accumulated rows.

TODO: implement `MertonError`, `dd` and `to_pd` in this file: the integer
distance over a tabulated band, and the world's own ladder walked by greatest
lower bound.

    `dd` refuses by name a band that is not one of the tabulated bands' upper
    bounds, a non-positive asset or debt, and an input that is not a whole
    number. `to_pd` refuses by name a distance below the ladder's first bound
    or above its last, and a distance that is not a whole number.
"""

import os
import sys

_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
_PATH = os.path.dirname(_DIR) if os.path.basename(_DIR) == "solutions" else _DIR
if _PATH not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, _PATH)

import claims as market

DD_SCALE = market.DD_SCALE


class MertonError(ValueError):
    """The refusal this stage raises: a credit the identity cannot measure.

    It names the offender — the band the table does not hold, the asset or
    debt that is not a count of cents, the distance the ladder does not walk
    to — because a distance nobody can grade must say what it was asked for
    rather than answer a probability nobody booked.
    """


def _whole(value, what):
    """A whole number, and a `bool` is not one here."""
    if isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, int):
        raise MertonError("the %s %r is a %s, not a whole number"
                          % (what, value, type(value).__name__))
    return value


def dd(asset_value, debt, band_bp):
    """The distance to default in whole band units, computed in integers.

    `(asset - debt) * DD_SCALE * DD_SCALE // (asset * band_bp)`: the equity
    cushion over the assets, measured against the band the identity books the
    borrower at. A borrower whose debt stands at or above its assets answers
    a negative distance and says so.

    A band that is not one of the tabulated bands' upper bounds, a
    non-positive asset or debt, or an input that is not a whole number, is
    refused by name.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 4: implement dd()")


def to_pd(dd_units):
    """The cumulative probability of default the distance maps to, in bp.

    The world's own `PD_LADDER`, walked the bank's way: the row whose
    `from_dd` is the greatest lower bound of the distance answers its
    `pd_bp`. A distance below the first bound or above the last is refused by
    name — the ladder's ends are the world's, not the stage's, and a
    probability invented beyond them would smooth what the world measured.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 4: implement to_pd()")

"""Distressed Debt Investing From Scratch — stage 5: The three values that disagree.

The fund underwrites a claim with three readings, and they never agree. The
first reads the bank's actuals (stage 3's walk): what the defaulted book on
the segment collected, haircutted and discounted — the recovery-based view.
The second reads the identity (stage 4's distance): the equity cushion over
the debt, the ladder it maps to, and the recovery the model expects the par
to be worth — the Merton-based view. The third reads the market (the
comparables table): what similar defaulted segments actually paid, in basis
points of par — the trading view.

`three(book, claim, at)` answers all three plus one more number the course
underwrites on: the MIDDLE of the three. A fund that underwrites on its best
case pays too much, and one that underwrites on its worst case never buys —
the consensus of two out of three views is the reading the trade clears or
fails, so the stage answers it in the record rather than making every later
stage re-derive it from the three legs.

`spread(...)` answers what each pair of readings leaves between itself and
the other — signed, in basis points of par. The gaps are the trade: the fund
sits between the readings, buys under the middle one's line at a discount to
the market's, and the check pins the gaps to the hundredth the divisions
leave, because a spread of one basis point at nine million of face is nine
hundred cents and nobody should lose them by rounding.

    THREE_KEYS                    the six fields of the three readings, in order
    SPREAD_KEYS                   the five fields of the pairwise gaps, in order
    ValuationError                the refusal this stage raises
    three(book, claim, at)        -> THREE_KEYS: the readings, and the middle
    spread(reading)               -> SPREAD_KEYS: what each pair leaves

DESIGN DECISION — why does the stage answer the middle rather than the three
alone?
Because the middle IS the underwriting decision, hiding it among three legs
keeps the decision implicit: every downstream stage would re-derive it,
mis-deriving it the first time a tie or a reordering arrives. The record
answers forecast, Merton, comparables and `middle_bp` — four numbers, one
claim, one date — and the check pins the middle to the sorted list's own
centre, so a stage that "decided" on the mean (a kind of average floats love
and integers refuse) or the best case shows as a disagreement with the
sorting.

DESIGN DECISION — why are the gaps signed rather than absolute?
Because direction is the information: the forecast sits under the Merton
reading and the Merton under the comparables — a borrower in the world's
actuals has been paid less than the model expects, and the model less than the
market pays for similar distress. Signed gaps turn that into arithmetic:
`forecast_merton_bp` is how far the actuals trail the model, and a check pins
each to its sign, so a walk that got the direction backwards shows immediately.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the Merton leg come from the entry date's asset
value, and refuse elsewhere on the path?
Because the reading is the fund's as of the day it decides: the asset path's
month end at `at` and the borrower's booked debt and band give the distance,
the ladder gives the probability, and the recovery is what the par is worth
when the borrower is not fully wiped out. A date off the path has no asset
reading — the world refuses it, and so does this stage — and a distance the
ladder cannot walk to (the close's asset value sinks the distance past even
the ladder's worst row) means the model has no answer for that borrower on
that day, which is a refusal and not a zero.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the equity refused and not priced?
Because the equity does ride a price on the sheet and a comparables row below
it, but no par: a recovery rate has no face to apply to, and the fund's
three-reading discipline is a debt discipline. Pricing the sponsor's claim by
the same machinery would answer a number that looks like the others and
cannot be defended like them — so the stage refuses by name, and the equity
rides the course's decisions only through the waterfall (stage 1) it sits
beneath.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the stage re-walk the bank's actuals instead of
importing stage 3's answer?
Because stages stand alone in this course: a stage reads the WORLD, never
another stage's output, and the three-reading record must be reproducible by
anyone holding the book and the claim — which is also what makes it
auditable. The walk is the same haircut-and-step arithmetic, written once
here, and the check pins it against its own re-walk, so the two files agree
or the course says so loudly.

three readings from the bank's actuals, the identity and the comparables
table; the middle of the three; and the signed gaps each pair leaves.

    The request is refused by name when the claim record carries no `kind`,
    `segment`, `collateral_kind` or `borrower`, when the kind is `equity`,
    when the identity books no borrower under the claim's name, when the
    `at` is not a date the asset path has a reading for, and when the
    comparables hold no row for the claim's segment and collateral. The
    spread is refused by name when the record it is asked to spread is not
    a `THREE_KEYS` record.
"""

import claims as market
import rules
import dates

PAR_BP = 10000

THREE_KEYS = ("claim", "at", "forecast_bp", "merton_bp", "comparables_bp",
              "middle_bp")

SPREAD_KEYS = ("claim", "at", "forecast_merton_bp", "forecast_comparables_bp",
               "merton_comparables_bp")


class ValuationError(ValueError):
    """The refusal this stage raises: a claim the three views cannot price.

    It names the offender — the claim, the borrower, the date, the segment
    and collateral the comparables do not carry — because a valuation the
    world cannot underwrite must say what it was asked for rather than answer
    three numbers and a middle nobody bought.
    """


def three(book, claim, at):
    """The three readings of one claim, and the middle the fund underwrites on.

    The recovery-based leg reads the bank's own defaulted book on the claim's
    segment, haircutted and discounted to `at` at each loan's own rate. The
    Merton-based leg reads the asset path at `at`, the borrower's booked debt
    and band, and the world's own ladder: the distance the identity answers,
    the probability it walks to, and the recovery the par is left with. The
    comparables-based leg reads the trading table's row for the claim's
    segment and collateral. The middle is the sorted three's own centre.

    A claim of kind `equity`, a record the book and the world cannot read, a
    date off the asset path, and a segment and collateral the comparables do
    not carry, are refused by name.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 5: implement three()")

    """What each pair of the three readings leaves, signed, in basis points.

    `forecast_merton_bp` is the forecast less the Merton reading;
    `forecast_comparables_bp` the forecast less the comparables; and
    `merton_comparables_bp` the Merton less the comparables. The three gaps
    are signed: a leg that sits below another answers the negative it is.

    A record that is not a `THREE_KEYS` record is refused by name.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 5: implement spread()")
files.stage_06.py:
"""Distressed Debt Investing From Scratch — stage 6: The restructuring waterfall against absolute priority.

The close the world settled is recorded: a pool of proceeds, the ballots, and
— the part this stage is about — the ABSOLUTE-PRIORITY BREAKS the parties
agreed. Each break names the class it paid, the cents it paid it, the line
ahead of which it was paid, and the rule it bent. This stage recomputes what
each class ACTUALLY received from those facts, and then names the
contradictions: the cents the waterfall would have paid, and the cents the
decree instead gave to or took from each class.

The recomputation is the stage-1 waterfall with one addition. The decree comes
first — the breaks' cents are lifted straight out of the pool, before any par
line is served — and then the remaining pool runs down `faces`: each debt
claim what remains after the classes above it, up to its face. The actual
received is decree plus waterfall. The identity the check pins holds to the
cent: every cent the settlement paid is either in the waterfall or in a named
break, and both walks answer from the same pool, so their sums agree — or
somebody's settlement pays more than it had, which is a refusal.

`violations(restructuring)` walks the same pool again with no decree at all —
the payment absolute priority WOULD have ordered — and answers one row per
break: the break's own four fields echoed, plus the signed difference the
decree made to the class it paid (`given_cents`) and to the class it bent
(`taken_cents`). For the world's settlement these are the same three million
six hundred thousand — given to the insurer's bonds, taken from the unsecured
pareach — because a decree that pays a class out of turn comes out of the
turn the next class had.

    S6_PAYMENT_KEYS               the six fields of one class's settlement, in order
    S6_VIOLATIONS_KEYS            the six fields of one named violation, in order
    PriorityError                 the refusal this stage raises
    settlement_payment(restructuring, claim_rank)

"""The tiny API an authored course uses to describe its stages.

A course is a directory containing `course.py`:

    from codecraft.api import stage

    TITLE = "Build a Bloom Filter"
    DESCRIPTION = "A probabilistic set, from hashing to false-positive math."

    def check_1():
        from bloom import BloomFilter
        bf = BloomFilter(bits=64, hashes=2)
        bf.add("x")
        assert "x" in bf
        assert "y" not in bf, "a fresh filter must not report false members"

    STAGES = [
        stage(
            1,
            file="bloom.py",
            title="add and contains",
            tags=["hashing", "data-structure"],
            action="Implement add() to set the k bit positions.",
            predict="can contains() ever be certain an item is absent?",
            hints=["bits = bits[:] to avoid shared state",
                   "use one hash salt per position"],
            check=check_1,
        ),
        ...
    ]

`codecraft run <course>` imports this file, runs each `check`, records the
attempt, and hands the result to the adaptive engine. `hints` are optional —
when omitted, the engine generates them from `action`/`predict`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional


@dataclass
class Stage:
    id: int
    file: str
    title: str
    check: Callable[[], None]
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action: str = ""
    predict: str = ""
    hints: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    solution: Optional[str] = None   # e.g. "solutions/bloom.py: BloomFilter.add"

    def meta(self) -> Dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "file": self.file,
            "title": self.title,
            "tags": list(self.tags),
            "action": self.action,
            "predict": self.predict,
            "hints": list(self.hints),
            "solution": self.solution,
        }


def stage(id: int, file: str, title: str, check: Callable[[], None],
          tags: Optional[List[str]] = None, action: str = "", predict: str = "",
          hints: Optional[List[str]] = None,
          solution: Optional[str] = None) -> Stage:
    """Convenience constructor so course.py stays readable."""
    return Stage(
        id=id, file=file, title=title, check=check, tags=list(tags or []),
        action=action, predict=predict, hints=list(hints or []),
        solution=solution,
    )
